I was sitting with my husband on the deck in an area where there was a chrome metal railing just a few inches high. It was windy and the boat moved quickly, and leaned quite severely. The angle felt very precarious and I could feel myself sliding. My husband struggled to hold on to me. I recall vividly looking at the churning water a couple of feet below and the little chrome rail and feeling sure I was going in.  I was frozen and couldn’t make a sound, just thought I should kick my shoes off so I can swim. After several minutes the boat righted itself and we turned back to the dock. These aren't public companies, so the normal securities disclosure regime doesn't even apply to them directly. Yet the SEC still caught a reported $20 billion in undisclosed affiliated-party loans that the Delaware Department of Insurance - the regulator with actual jurisdiction over these insurers - apparently missed for years.

Two Dodd-Frank provisions set the table for exactly this kind of structure. The 2010 Harkin Amendment blocked the SEC's Rule 151A and kept indexed annuities under state-only oversight, by design. And Dodd-Frank's reinsurance credit reform handed sole authority over reinsurance collateral requirements to a single state - the ceding insurer's domicile - which is exactly the dynamic that let captive-friendly states compete toward lighter collateral rules. That's what made the offshore/onshore captive reinsurance trick so attractive to PE-owned insurers in the first place: cede reserves to an affiliate, post minimal real collateral, and call it capital.

Fifty-one state regulators, no consolidated view of an insurer group's related-party lending, and it took an agency with a completely different mandate to notice a multibillion-dollar concealment that Delaware had every tool to catch and didn't.

Walter hasn't been charged with anything. But the system that was supposed to catch this before it reached $20 billion was built with the cracks already in it.

A great many young men have no form to their lives, no sequence of obligations telling them who they are on a Tuesday afternoon. The priesthood offers exactly that. It is a real need and I do not mock it. But it is not a vocation.

The accounting comes later, at fifty-five, when a life without children or partner comes due. The obvious answer is that such a man leaves, as thousands did in the seventies. But the men most likely to have entered for this reason are the least able to. Someone who needed a frame built around him at twenty-two cannot build one from nothing at fifty-five. He stays, and the reckoning happens anyway, with nowhere to go.

A man in that position looks for who took it from him. There will be no shortage of people ready with an answer.

That is what to watch for, thirty years out. Not a crisis of faith. A cohort of men who signed up for order, learned too late what it charged, could not leave, and arrive in late middle age angry and available and who turn to the right.

Despite countless billions of taxpayer dollars being spent, we have never even come close to a system that would defend against ICBM's.
Ultimately, US national security would have been far better served had Reagan taken the deal rather than imaging that there was a technical solution to this human problem.

On a personal note: I went door to door with a TV crew in Baltimore while the summit was underway asking people how they felt about the Reagan/Gorbachev meeting. Overwhelmingly, normal American citizens expressed that their greatest hope was that the two leaders would reduce the threat of global annihilation. As it stands, they made progress but each and every day we still remain less than 30 minutes from total destruction.

But it pushes the false argument that Reagan's military buildup led to Gorbachev being so flexible. I talked to a scholar who had read Gorbachev's papers, and there is nothing in those papers about his being motivated by the American buildup.

Also, the movie makes no mention of the movie The Day After about the effects of a nuclear war. It had great influence on Reagan.

As for being on the "brink of war," the Russians had no interest is such a war and were struggling on many fronts. We were not on the brink of war!

He was an actor who acted his way through the presidency and his best lines were written for him. Mikhail Gorbachev, on the other hand, was underplayed and a bit unfair, IMHO.  Where is the man who willingly dismantled the Soviet Union and set millions of Eastern Europeans free? Where is the perestroika and glasnost? Why is Reagan allowed to presciently say "Tear down the wall" (though not referring to Berlin, at the time), while Gorbachev is portrayed as the uncompromising deal breaker?

comments.name: Debbie Fields

The work was inspiring, as were the many brilliant people that I worked with. One of my many assignments was to simulate massive attacks on the US from the USSR. Our ground rules required that we would not strike first. So the objective was to protect enough fire power, and also command and control facilities to strike back. In order to make these simulations, I had to study nuclear effects, including a whole lot of detailed classified information. The nightmares came much later. Once during a huge thunderstorm I woke up thinking that the end of the world had arrived. I sat on the edge of the bed for a long time, just trying to breath.
